title: Backbase Launches Conversational Banking To Bring Agentic AI To Bank Customer Service
excerpt: . Backbase Launches Conversational Banking To Bring Agentic AI To Bank Customer Service. Backbase has launched Conversational Banking in general availability, an agentic AI offering that lets bank customers and employees use natural-language conversations to initiate and complete banking tasks while operating within institution-defined permissions, policies, and approval requirements. The new capability runs on Backbase’s AI-native Banking OS and is designed to move digital banking beyond providing customers with access to information and toward allowing AI agents to execute approved actions on their behalf. Customers can use voice or text to describe what they need without navigating through multiple menus or workflows. For example, a customer could ask to block and replace a lost card, check the status of a payment or advance an existing service request. Backbase’s AI agents interpret the request, use available customer context and connect with relevant banking systems to complete actions the bank has authorized them to perform. When a request requires investigation, an exception or human judgment, the platform can transfer the matter to an employee along with relevant customer information and a summary of the work the AI agent has already completed. The approach aims to reduce repetitive information gathering and give employees more time to handle advisory conversations and complex customer requirements. Backbase sees Conversational Banking as part of a broader shift from traditional digital self-service toward agentic banking, where AI systems can take action rather than simply provide answers. The company cited McKinsey & Company estimates indicating that agentic AI could reduce banking operating costs by between 15% and 20% by automating routine requests and reducing repeated information gathering. Backbase is building governance directly into how its agents execute banking tasks. Financial institutions determine which information, knowledge and tools an AI agent can access, which actions it is permitted to perform and which activities require human approval. Consequential requests also require explicit confirmation from the customer before they are completed. The platform maintains records covering the context surrounding requests, checks performed, decisions made and eventual outcomes, giving banks an auditable history of agent activity. This governance model is designed to allow financial institutions to introduce more autonomous AI capabilities without giving up control over customer interactions or regulated banking processes. Conversational Banking is already operating in production at more than 10 banks. Backbase said one of South Africa’s four largest banks has used the technology across 22 million customer interactions while increasing its self-service containment rate from 20% to 70%. Meriwest has also deployed Backbase’s conversational AI and reported savings through increased automation and call containment alongside improvements to the customer service experience. At VeraBank, the technology has been used to consolidate multiple information sources into a searchable environment where employees can ask questions and retrieve information needed to assist customers. Backbase designed Conversational Banking to operate alongside banks’ existing technology stacks. Institutions do not have to replace their current online or mobile banking platforms to begin using the technology. Instead, a bank can initially deploy Conversational Banking for selected use cases, connect the systems needed for those workflows and establish the permissions and controls governing how the agents operate. That approach gives banks the ability to gradually increase the range of activities handled by AI agents as they gain operational experience with the technology. title: AI threats weren't a top concern for Canada's banking regulator, but a lot has changed in 6 months
excerpt: . AI threats weren't a top concern for Canada's banking regulator, but a lot has changed in 6 months. Naimul Karim. Thu, October 8, 2026 at 11:28 a. m. CDT 4 min read. Threats linked to artificial intelligence were not one of the top concerns for Canada's banking regulator in April, when it released its annual risk outlook, but a series of incidents in the past six months have now led it to elevate the risks that financial institutions face due to AI. "Recent stories about how agents are at least interpreting their task authorizations liberally and potentially posing dangers to institutions — that's frightening," Peter Routledge, head of the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), said at a press conference on Wednesday. "That is a risk front and centre for us. AI has sort of moved along the capabilities curve. ". He was referring to how frontier models of AI companies in the United States such as Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Inc. went rogue in the past few months and tried to hack other organizations. As a result, OSFI is mulling over whether Canada's financial system requires an AI safety code. Routledge did not provide details on what such a code would look like, but said the main goal would be to improve the ability of financial institutions to tackle threats linked to AI. "Maybe play a useful role in elevating basic standards to a minimum level, so we have some semblance of confidence that across the financial system there's a basic level of safety and protection," he said. "I am using the words 'safety code' as sort of emblematic of that. We haven't developed it. I don't have a draft of it. I have asked my team to start thinking about it. ". But Routledge said he's satisfied with how prepared Canada's banks are to tackle AI-related threats, though not all institutions are at the same level, so he's looking to establish a minimum level of safety for all the institutions OSFI supervises because of the high level of interconnectivity in the financial sector. "You are connected to your counterparties, and if there's poison at the counterparties, it's flowing through to you as an institution," he said. "Our highest utility is to try and lessen the risk that scatters around the system. ". OSFI, in its semi-annual risk report released on Thursday, said advances in AI have increased the "effectiveness, speed and sophistication of malicious cyberattacks. ". It said frontier AI models can chain together multiple vulnerabilities across systems that are connected, allowing seemingly minor weaknesses to be combined to launch high-impact attacks. The advances in AI, which is likely to continue, also mean institutions have less time to detect and respond to threats. The majority of the top AI companies are situated outside Canada, and as financial institutions rely on their services, cross-border dependencies will likely increase, the report said. "Geopolitical tensions, including technology restrictions and policy actions in foreign jurisdictions, could affect access to critical technologies and services," it said. The report also said it is also important to ensure that governance, controls and testing evolve at a similar pace as institutions use AI technologies to improve their businesses. title: Singapore's Central Bank Requires Independent Review for All FinTech AI Deployments
excerpt: . # Regulation. Singapore's Central Bank Requires Independent Review for All FinTech AI Deployments. Oct 8, 2026, 4:05 AM UTC •. Lukas Brandt. • 2 min read. Share this article. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has issued its first AI risk management guidelines for financial institutions, mandating independent review of all AI use cases before deployment and holding firms accountable for third-party AI failures. Singapore's Monetary Authority (MAS) published its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions on Wednesday, requiring all local financial firms to submit AI use cases for independent review before putting them into production. The guidelines take effect October 7, 2027, giving institutions a year to comply. MAS acts as both central bank and financial regulator for the island nation, which has become a global finance hub through a combination of strict regulation and low taxes. "The use of AI can improve performance across business and functional areas but its complexity and probabilistic nature can lead to greater uncertainty, as well as unexpected or more biased behaviour that is harder to identify compared to the use of simpler methods," the guidelines state. MAS rates generative AI as riskier than traditional AI models. The regulator cites noise in training data, unrepresentative training data, and encounters with scenarios absent from training data as sources of risk. Agentic AI, MAS warns, "could further amplify these risks. ". The guidelines require boards and senior management to expand risk management frameworks to cover AI. Before deployment, financial institutions must subject each AI use case — including underlying systems and models — to review by parties not involved in development. Technology and cybersecurity reviews must also confirm that AI can enter production environments in a controlled and secure manner. Ongoing monitoring of both proprietary systems and third-party AI services is mandatory. "Given the uncertainties associated with AI, their dynamic nature and the potential for model staleness and performance degradation due to data or model drifts over time, ongoing monitoring is critical to ensure that deployed AI operates as intended and remains fit for purpose over time," the guidelines state. MAS rejects third-party failures as an excuse. "FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties," the regulator said. Firms must obtain sufficient assurance from providers, assess suitability, and apply compensating controls where gaps exist. If risks exceed the institution's risk appetite, the firm should limit, suspend, or replace the third-party AI service. Institutions must maintain current inventories of all AI used in their business. When third-party services use AI without disclosure, firms must find ways to manage the risk of unknown AI contributions. Contingency plans and fallback options — including alternative systems or manual processes — are required for high-risk AI applications to ensure business continuity during AI failure or unexpected behavior. The guidelines reflect Singapore's approach to maintaining its status as a premier financial center while addressing emerging technology risks. Financial institutions operating in Singapore now face a clear compliance deadline and specific operational requirements for AI governance. title: HCLTech Study Reveals Wealth Management Firms Unprepared For AI Transition
excerpt: . Home » Business » HCLTech Study Reveals Wealth Management Firms Unprepared For AI Transition. HCLTech Study Reveals Wealth Management Firms Unprepared For AI Transition. Source: PTI - Edited By: Rediff Money Desk September 28, 2026 19:54 IST 3 Minutes Read. x. A recent HCLTech study reveals a significant gap in AI preparedness among global wealth management firms, highlighting critical blind spots hindering effective digital transformation and measurable business outcomes. IMAGE: Illustration: Dado Ruvic/Reuters. Key Points. 84% of global wealth management firms acknowledge the need for AI-driven operating model redesign. Less than 10% of these firms are currently prepared for the necessary AI transition. HCLTech's study, 'Hidden In Pl(AI)n Sight', identifies three critical "blind spots": ambition, execution, and strategy. Geographic variations show APAC and North America more confident in AI readiness than Europe. Future industry leaders are expected to excel at orchestrating AI capabilities with human expertise. As many as 84 per cent of global wealth management firms acknowledge that their operating models require a fundamental redesign to realise the promise of artificial intelligence (AI), but less than 10 per cent are prepared for the transition, according to a study released on Monday by IT services major HCLTech. Key Findings From HCLTech Report. The report, titled 'Hidden In Pl(AI)n Sight', revealed that while 98 per cent of leadership teams in the wealth management sector are actively pursuing an AI agenda, slightly over 7 per cent are actively building agentic AI capabilities. In an interesting twist, HCLTech surveyed 1,066 "representative AI personas" modelled on senior wealth management decision-makers across 17 global markets for the research. Identifying Critical Blind Spots. The findings highlighted three critical blind spots hindering firms from converting AI initiatives into measurable business outcomes: an "ambition blind spot", where firms recognise transformation needs but only fund efficiency gains; an "execution blind spot", where tech investments are not matched by investments in proprietary client data and insights; and a "strategy blind spot", where institutions track AI adoption rather than its impact on growth and revenue. "The industry doesn't have an investment problem. It has a choice problem. Nearly every wealth management firm is spending on AI. Far fewer can say which programmes they are funding, how far AI actually reaches into the operating model, or whether they're measuring the outcomes that matter - new client value, growth and revenue models," said Srinivasan Seshadri, Chief Growth Officer and Global Head of Financial Services, HCLTech. Regional Readiness And Future Outlook. The report noted significant geographic variations in readiness and confidence. The Asia-Pacific (APAC) region led with 89 per cent confidence, followed closely by North America at 84 per cent, whereas Europe lagged significantly at 38. 3 per cent. Executives surveyed ranked first-party and behavioural data as more critical differentiators than technology infrastructure, cloud platforms, or external AI partnerships. Additionally, nearly 80 per cent of respondents believe future industry leaders will be those who best orchestrate AI capabilities alongside human expertise and ecosystem partners. title: HSBC Plans ‘Brutal’ UK Wealth Job Cuts as AI Restructuring Accelerates
excerpt: . Back to News / Business. Build your reading streak 0 / 3 today · Counts at 25%. HSBC is preparing to eliminate dozens of roles across its UK wealth management division as the bank accelerates its reliance on artificial intelligence to streamline operations and reduce costs. The proposed restructuring, described in internal communications as a 'brutal' cull, is expected to affect relationship managers and specialist staff as chief executive Georges Elhedery pushes forward with a sweeping transformation of the lender's global footprint. The move underscores a broader industry trend where major financial institutions are deploying AI to automate client services, compliance checks, and portfolio management, fundamentally altering the traditional banking employment model. According to reports from the Financial Times, HSBC plans deep cuts in its UK wealth business as it leans heavily on automated capabilities to service clients. Hundreds of people are currently employed as wealth relationship managers at the bank across the UK, and the planned restructuring is expected to affect a significant portion of these roles as the bank seeks to flatten its organizational hierarchy. The cuts are part of a wider effort to improve the bank's return on tangible equity, a metric that has remained a focal point for Elhedery since he assumed the chief executive position in September 2024. The Strategic Pivot Toward Automation. The strategic pivot toward artificial intelligence has been a cornerstone of Elhedery’s tenure. Earlier this year, the chief executive explicitly urged staff not to fight the rise of artificial intelligence, acknowledging that the technology would inevitably destroy certain administrative and middle-office roles while creating new technical positions. This philosophy is already manifesting in the bank's operational geography. In July 2026, HSBC announced plans to establish a Global AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore, intending to hire over 100 AI specialists alongside new wealth managers in that region, highlighting a deliberate shift of high-value technical roles away from traditional Western financial hubs. The automation of wealth management extends far beyond simple customer service chatbots. Modern machine learning algorithms are now capable of processing vast datasets to generate personalized investment insights, predict client churn, and automate the increasingly burdensome regulatory requirements associated with Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) protocols. These back-office and middle-office functions have historically employed large numbers of graduates and compliance specialists. By integrating large language models and predictive analytics, HSBC aims to drastically reduce the manual hours required to onboard high-net-worth clients and monitor their portfolios for risk exposure. Industry Pressures and the Hybrid Model. However, the transition is not without significant operational risks. Industry analysts note that while AI excels at data processing and routine portfolio rebalancing, high-net-worth individuals still demand human interaction for complex tax planning, cross-border succession planning, and behavioral coaching during periods of market volatility. Consequently, the bank is likely pursuing a hybrid model, where the remaining human relationship managers are expected to oversee larger client books, utilizing AI as an augmented tool rather than a replacement. This shift places immense pressure on surviving staff to demonstrate value in complex advisory services that algorithms cannot easily replicate, effectively raising the performance baseline for the entire division. The push for technological efficiency at HSBC mirrors aggressive restructuring efforts across the global banking sector. NEW DELHI: Union Minister for Electronics and IT Ashwini Vaishnaw on Thursday launched the World Bank Group’s "World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence " at an event organised by the IndiaAI Mission and MeitY. The study found that AI can widen access to expertise, raise productivity, and improve the delivery of services in developing economies. AI-enabled tools are already being deployed in medical screening, agricultural decision-making and education, extending scarce expertise to larger sections of the population. The report further emphasises that these gains rest on strong foundations, including reliable electricity and connectivity, computing infrastructure, quality data, skills, education systems and capable institutions. Advt. "AI is changing the lives of ordinary people. In Baramati, sugarcane yields rose by 40 per cent with 30 per cent less water and fertiliser, for farmers who have never used a computer simply through voice on a phone," said Vaishnaw. The Minister added that in healthcare, tuberculosis detection has increased by 35 per cent, demonstrating how AI applications can transform lives across the Global South. He noted that the Baramati initiative draws on satellite, IoT, and weather data while lowering labour costs, alongside Gujarat's AgriStack serving 5 lakh farmers and the Sarlaben AI livestock platform benefiting 3 crore cattle. Through the IndiaAI Mission, the government is establishing a comprehensive AI ecosystem across seven pillars, including compute capacity, the IndiaAI Innovation Centre for foundation models, dataset platforms, startup financing, and safe AI. The Safe & Trusted AI pillar supports indigenous tools for responsible AI deployment, focusing on bias mitigation, algorithm auditing, explainable AI, privacy-preserving frameworks, deepfake detection, and institutional safety governance. "One of the key messages of the World Development Report is not about creating artificial intelligence but deploying it. India has a unique opportunity to bring together institutions, markets and AI to transform millions of lives," said Somik Lall, director of strategy, development economics at World Bank Group. Advt. World Bank Chief Economist Michael Kremer highlighted India's AI-based monsoon forecasting model, tested across multiple open-access models and delivered via text and voice, noting that countries like Ethiopia are now adopting India's approach. "India is already approaching the path of AI for development by adapting tools to local contexts with the government playing the role of an enabler, user and regulator of this new technology," said Gaurav Nayyar, director, World Development Report 2026. "The World Development Report aligns closely with India’s AI roadmap compute, data and models and sets out a sensible approach to regulation: rely on existing laws and voluntary compliance, and revisit regulation as the technology evolves," said S Krishnan , secretary at MeitY. Krishnan added that work is under way on an AI Talent Mission to build human capabilities, positioning India’s high AI skill penetration to support wider enterprise adoption and Global South development goals. title: Advanced AI models amplify risk in the financial system, banking regulator says
excerpt: Comments. Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create an account. Listen to this article. Learn more about audio. Log in or Create an account to listen to this article. Canada’s banking regular is warning that rapid AI development is amplifying cybersecurity and technology sovereignty risks in the country’s financial system. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions highlighted AI risks in its fall update on the biggest threats facing the banking sector. The regulator said the pace of AI development has “accelerated materially” since it unveiled its annual risk outlook in April. The rate of change in frontier models is “unprecedented” and the time between discovering a vulnerability and potential exploitation of that gap has shortened, reducing the time that financial institutions have to identify the risk and address it, OSFI said. “In an era of advancing AI capabilities, resilience is a competitive advantage,” OSFI superintendent Peter Routledge said in a statement released with the fall update Thursday. “Financial institutions that harness AI responsibly while managing cyber, technology, and third-party risks will position themselves to thrive in a complex environment. ”. On Wednesday, Mr. Routledge told a room of financial institution risk professionals that the regulator is planning to implement an AI “safety code” as threats from AI agents and Anthropic’s powerful Claude Mythos model escalate risks among the country’s banks. While the initiative is still in its earlier stages, he said the guidelines could consist of broad, high-level standards that provide a basic level of safety and protection for the financial system, while also establishing a “wide perimeter for innovation. ”. Canadian banks been increasingly conducting AI research and implementing tools that boost productivity and generate revenue. On Tuesday, AI benchmarking platform Evident ranked all of Canada’s five biggest banks among the top 30 in a list of 50 global financial institutions on AI adoption. But advances in AI also increase the speed and sophistication of cyberattacks, which could allow weaknesses that seem minor to be exploited for high-impact attacks, OSFI said in the fall update. “Frontier AI models can locate and exploit more vulnerabilities, enabling adversaries to launch coordinated, large-scale attacks across systems, applications, and third-party ecosystems,” the regulator said. Risks to Canada’s technology sovereignty are also on the rise, according to the fall update. The development of frontier models is dominated by a small group of providers, and many are concentrated outside of Canada. Escalating geopolitical tensions, including technology restrictions and policy actions in foreign markets, could affect access to technology and services for Canada’s institutions, OSFI said. OSFI has been recently ratcheting up its oversight of AI. In 2023, the regulator and the Global Risk Institute released a report on the implications of AI for financial services institutions. OSFI has also previously cited AI as a key threat in its annual risk outlook. Earlier this year, the regulator unveiled two technology risk bulletins on generative and agentic AI and frontier AI and listed ways to strengthen resilience against vulnerabilities. title: World Bank: AI Offers Historic Opportunity For Developing Countries
excerpt: . Home » Business » World Bank: AI Offers Historic Opportunity For Developing Countries. World Bank: AI Offers Historic Opportunity For Developing Countries. Source: PTI - Edited By: Rediff Money Desk October 08, 2026 20:12 IST 3 Minutes Read. Discover how the World Bank's latest report, 'The Promise of Artificial Intelligence', outlines a "historic opportunity" for low- and middle-income countries to leverage AI for development, despite current preparedness gaps. IMAGE: Illustration: Dado Ruvic/Reuters. Key Points. AI offers a "historic opportunity" for low- and middle-income countries to address development challenges, though many are currently unprepared. Developing nations should prioritise adopting and adapting existing AI tools for local needs before attempting to build their own frontier models. Building frontier AI models is "not a realistic goal in the near future" for most developing countries, with only a few making inroads like India's Sarvam AI. AI is spreading rapidly, with middle-income countries accounting for half of ChatGPT's global traffic within six months of its launch. The immediate risk of job disruption from generative AI in low- and middle-income countries is limited to a small share of knowledge-intensive jobs, while AI can enhance small businesses. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents a "historic opportunity" for low- and middle-income countries to overcome long-standing development challenges, but the countries with the most to gain are the least prepared, according to a World Bank report. AI's Promise for Developing Nations. The World Development Report 2026, titled 'The Promise of Artificial Intelligence', said developing countries should first adopt existing AI tools and adapt to them for local needs before advancing to build their own frontier models. Building frontier models is "not a realistic goal in the near future" for most developing countries, the report said. "Only a small number of countries and companies have the resources to compete at that level, and progress might take years. A few countries are making inroads. Examples include India's Sarvam AI, the United Arab Emirates' Falcon, and Sub-Saharan Africa's InkubaLM, which were built from scratch to work better in local languages," it said. Bridging the AI Adoption Gap. The report said AI was spreading faster than earlier technologies. Within six months of ChatGPT's launch, middle-income countries accounted for half of its global traffic. The gap in usage, however, remains wide. By April 2025, nearly 25 per cent of internet users in high-income countries had adopted ChatGPT, compared with 4. 7 per cent in lower-middle-income countries and 0. 7 per cent in low-income countries. About 4. 5 per cent of jobs in low- and middle-income countries can be automated by generative AI, against 14. 2 per cent in high-income countries, the report said. "In developing countries, the immediate risk of disruption from AI is limited to a small share of jobs, involving people employed in knowledge-intensive professional services. On the flip side, AI has the potential to improve the capabilities of many small businesses, in which most people are currently employed and in which they undertake manual rather than cognitive work," it said. New Delhi: Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, the Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology, Railways, and Information and Broadcasting, today launched the World Bank Group’s World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence at an event held at The Oberoi, New Delhi. The Report examines the opportunities and challenges that Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents for developing economies, and sets out a framework for countries to harness AI for development through adoption, adaptation and advancement. The launch was organised by the IndiaAI Mission, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, in collaboration with the World Bank Group. It brought together senior policymakers, global development experts, technology leaders and practitioners to deliberate on how India can maximise, and safely sustain, the development gains from AI. The programme also featured a State AI Showcase, in which States and innovators presented AI-enabled solutions from across the country. The Report notes that AI can widen access to expertise, raise productivity and improve the delivery of services in developing economies. AI-enabled tools are already being deployed in medical screening, agricultural decision-making and education, extending scarce expertise to larger sections of the population. The Report further emphasises that these gains rest on strong foundations, including reliable electricity and connectivity, computing infrastructure, quality data, skills, education systems and capable institutions. Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, Union Minister of Electronics and IT delivered the keynote address and formally presented the Report. The Union Minister underlined India’s approach of democratising technology, so that the benefits of Artificial Intelligence reach citizens, enterprises and institutions across the country. “AI is changing the lives of ordinary people. In Baramati, sugarcane yields rose by 40 per cent with 30 per cent less water and fertiliser, for farmers who have never used a computer simply through voice on a phone. In healthcare, TB detection has increased by 35 per cent. Examples like these can change lives across the Global South and the world,” said Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw. The Union Minister added that the Baramati initiative draws on satellite, IoT and weather data and has also lowered labour costs. In Gujarat, AgriStack is being used by 5 lakh farmers, and AI for animal health through Sarlaben is benefiting 3 crore cattle and their farmers. India has emerged as a significant ecosystem for the development and deployment of AI, with applications in healthcare, agriculture, education, governance, financial services and other sectors of public and economic importance. Through the IndiaAI Mission, the Government of India is building a comprehensive AI ecosystem across seven pillars: IndiaAI Compute Capacity, IndiaAI Innovation Centre for indigenous foundation models, IndiaAI Datasets Platform (AIKosh), IndiaAI Application Development Initiative, IndiaAI FutureSkills, IndiaAI Startup Financing, and Safe & Trusted AI. The Mission seeks to strengthen India’s capabilities across the AI value chain, while ensuring that AI development remains inclusive, responsible and suited to India’s scale, diversity and multilingual context. The Government’s approach focuses on democratising access to compute, data and models, addressing India-specific challenges, and creating economic and employment opportunities. title: HSBC job cuts: Bank to axe UK roles amid AI push
excerpt: . Posted on October 7, 2026 by staff. HSBC job cuts: Bank to axe UK roles amid AI push. Bank could cut around 70% of financial adviser roles as chief exec Georges Elhedery puts artificial intelligence at heart of efficiency drive. Share:. Listen to article. HSBC is reportedly planning sweeping job cuts across its UK wealth management operation as it increases its use of artificial intelligence. The banking giant could cut around half of management and specialist roles in the division, while the number of financial advisers could be reduced by about 70%, according to the Financial Times. HSBC is currently consulting staff over the proposed changes, with affected employees expected to leave at the end of October. The bank did not disclose how many people work specifically in its UK wealth business, although it is thought to have hundreds of relationship managers around the country. The restructuring comes as group chief executive Georges Elhedery (pictured) makes greater use of AI and digital technology a central part of his efforts to simplify the bank and improve efficiency. At an investor event in May, Elhedery warned that “generative AI will destroy certain jobs” and said employees would need to embrace the changes brought about by the technology. HSBC has already introduced AI tools for its relationship managers. Elhedery said in July that the technology was being used to help staff serve customers more quickly, including providing market insights and personalised investment strategies. The reported cuts would represent a significant change in direction for HSBC, which launched a recruitment drive two years ago to expand its UK wealth and private banking operations. IKEA launches second-hand marketplace in UK. “HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider,” the bank said in a statement reported by the FT. “We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers. ”. HSBC’s UK wealth operation has around £134 billion of invested assets and wealth deposits across its premier and private banking businesses. Elhedery has been pursuing a wider cost-cutting programme since becoming chief executive in 2024, with the bank already stripping out $1. 5bn (£1. 13bn) of costs ahead of schedule. title: OSFI warns AI could amplify cyber and technology risks for lenders
excerpt: . ✕ Menu EN. FR. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Search. Written by CMT Team • October 8, 2026 • 3:57 PM • Government and Regulation • Views: 175. Written by. CMT Team. Government and Regulation. October 8, 2026. OSFI warns AI could amplify cyber and technology risks for lenders. The regulator says oversight and cyber defences need to keep pace as financial institutions adopt more advanced AI. Canada’s banking regulator is warning that growing reliance on a small number of AI and cloud providers could leave financial institutions exposed to disruptions affecting several firms at once. In its fall risk outlook , released Thursday, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions said a cyber incident, outage or operational failure at a major provider could have consequences across the financial sector. “As a result, third-party concentration risk may pose challenges to operational resilience as AI adoption expands,” the regulator said. With many technology services based outside Canada, OSFI said greater AI adoption is likely to deepen financial institutions’ reliance on foreign providers, leaving them more exposed to technology restrictions or policy decisions in other countries. OSFI said AI is making cyberattacks faster and more sophisticated, while putting capabilities that once required significant technical expertise within reach of a broader range of attackers. Advanced systems can identify and combine weaknesses across interconnected networks, turning seemingly minor vulnerabilities into more damaging attacks. That leaves institutions less time to detect threats and respond, although the same technology can also help strengthen cyber defences. Oversight needs to keep pace. OSFI said financial institutions may find it increasingly difficult to keep track of how their critical service providers use AI, the vulnerabilities that arise and the controls in place to manage them. That makes ongoing monitoring and oversight of those relationships more important. The regulator also acknowledged AI’s potential to improve productivity and risk management, while emphasizing that governance, controls and testing need to advance alongside adoption. Boards and senior management remain accountable for managing the risks. “In an era of advancing AI capabilities, resilience is a competitive advantage,” Superintendent Peter Routledge said in an accompanying release. “Financial institutions that harness AI responsibly while managing cyber, technology, and third-party risks will position themselves to thrive in a complex environment. ”. The update maintains OSFI’s focus on real estate secured lending, including mortgages, non-bank financial institutions and funding and liquidity risks. While economic uncertainty and geopolitical tensions continue to weigh on the operating environment, the regulator said federally regulated financial institutions remain resilient and profitable.
